title: Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia’s Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2021
short_title: Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia’s Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2021

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would change the Fair Work Act 2009 and related laws to help Australia recover from the COVID-19 pandemic.
It would introduce a legal definition of a casual employee, add a casual conversion right to the National Employment Standards, and extend temporary JobKeeper flexibilities for two years.
The explanatory memorandum says the bill would also require the Fair Work Commission to approve enterprise agreements within 21 working days where practicable.
changes: Introduces a statutory definition of casual employee.
Creates a right for regular casual employees to request conversion to permanent employment.
Extends temporary JobKeeper flexibilities for two years for employers in identified industries.
Streamlines the enterprise agreement approval process.
Strengthens compliance and enforcement frameworks for wage underpayments.
Sunsets pre-Fair Work Act agreements by 1 July 2022.
summary.affected: Employers, employees, unions, and the Fair Work Commission.

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: The Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill was introduced to support economic recovery from COVID-19, including a statutory definition of casual employment, a new casual conversion entitlement, award simplification for 12 identified awards, enterprise bargaining reforms, doubling the maximum nominal expiry date for greenfields agreements on major projects to eight years, and a new criminal offence for dishonest systematic wage underpayments with increased penalties.

speeches.speaker: Tony Burke
speeches.brief: The Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 fails to deliver secure jobs and decent pay, and attacks job security and wages through provisions on casuals, enterprise bargaining, award changes, and wage theft penalties. A second reading amendment was moved noting the bill makes jobs less secure and results in pay cuts.

speeches.speaker: Katrina Allen
speeches.brief: The Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 introduces a statutory definition of casual employment, stronger casual conversion rights, and a fix for double-dipping estimated at $39 billion in employer liability, along with award flexibilities, enterprise bargaining reforms, eight-year greenfield agreements for projects over $500 million, and $47.3 million in new compliance funding including tougher penalties for underpayments.

speeches.speaker: Daniel Mulino
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 would increase insecure work, lower wages growth, and worsen conditions for vulnerable workers, contrary to the government's claim of seeking consensus. They stated the bill fails because it reduces bargaining power, citing the ACTU's opposition, and highlighted that casual employment grew by 400,000 between May and November 2020, while the government's own figures show the bill would cancel an estimated $18 billion in entitlements.

speeches.speaker: George Christensen
speeches.brief: The speaker urged support for the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020, arguing casual workers doing the same work as permanent employees for over 12 months should have the right to convert to permanent roles. He blamed the Labor Party, including Murray Watt, for previously blocking this reform in 2019.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 fails to reduce casualisation, forces workers to go to the Federal Court to assert permanent status, and undermines existing state wage theft laws in Victoria and Queensland while reducing penalties.

speeches.speaker: Lucy Wicks
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020, which defines casual employment, creates a pathway to permanent roles, extends workplace flexibility for hard-hit industries, and introduces criminal penalties for wage theft. The speaker cited over 32,000 casual employees on the Central Coast and 2.3 million nationally, and noted a $12.9 million employer advisory service.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 was argued to be overdue, commonsense industrial relations reform needed to support economic recovery, with the speaker citing specific provisions: making the COVID-19 public interest exception permanent, creating a pathway for long-term casuals to move to permanent work, reducing enterprise agreement approval times to 21 days, and allowing greenfield agreements a nominal expiry date of up to eight years. The speaker also claimed most enterprise agreements are about 46 per cent better than awards and criticised opposition objections as robotic and harmful to employers.

speeches.speaker: Meryl Swanson
speeches.brief: The bill will leave workers worse off by cutting bargaining rights, undermining the Fair Work Commission, and increasing casualisation, with over 2,000 casual grocery workers and 1,800 fast food workers in the Paterson electorate affected.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the government's Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 would cut wages and conditions, and that the government only backed down on removing the better off overall test due to Labor and union pressure. The speaker also outlined Labor's eight principles for secure work, higher pay, and fairer conditions, including inserting job security into the Fair Work Act, rights for gig economy workers, and a crackdown on labour hire firms.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: The removal of the better off overall test (BOOT) from the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 was the most egregious aspect, as it would allow employers to vary employee conditions so they are no longer better off, and was likened to the Work Choices legislation.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 would allow pay cuts, make casualisation easier, extend greenfield agreements without pay rises for eight years, and override state wage theft laws, while noting the Prime Minister refused to guarantee no worker would be worse off. The speaker announced Labor would vote against the bill.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Phillips
speeches.brief: The member for Gilmore opposed the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020, arguing it would cut workers’ pay, increase casualisation, reduce job security, and harm the seasonal tourism economy of the New South Wales South Coast. She specifically criticised provisions that would allow additional hours without overtime, extend temporary COVID-19 stand-down directions, and weaken enterprise bargaining protections, warning the bill would disproportionately affect essential workers, women, and young people.

speeches.speaker: Emma McBride
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020, arguing it would increase job insecurity and cut pay by redefining casual work, retrospectively offsetting casual loading against permanent entitlements (cancelling an estimated $18–39 billion in back pay), and weakening conversion pathways. They also criticised the secretive working-group process and highlighted the bill's potential negative mental health impacts, especially as COVID-19 support like JobKeeper is wound back.

speeches.speaker: Anne Stanley
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2020 would make workers worse off by entrenching casualisation, noting that 60,000 workers in Werriwa would be affected through lost conditions and job security. The speech also criticised the government for failing to address stagnant real wages, which were almost one per cent lower in 2019 than in 2013, and for allowing employers to control conversion to permanent roles.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2020 will harm workers who were essential during COVID-19, making jobs more insecure and allowing pay cuts, while criticising the government for refusing to guarantee no worker would be worse off and for misrepresenting casual conversion provisions.

speeches.speaker: Ged Kearney
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 fails to address insecure work and instead makes it easier to employ casuals, while criticising the government for a history of attacking workers' rights, including Work Choices, penalty rate cuts, and the ensuring integrity bill. They stated the bill would not be supported, citing specific flaws such as enabling casualisation, complicating bargaining, allowing wage cuts, and weakening wage theft punishments in Victoria.

speeches.speaker: Josh Burns
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work Amendment Bill's title is misleading and criticised the government for pulling the Clean Energy Finance Corporation Amendment Bill after the member for New England introduced an undisclosed amendment.

speeches.speaker: Josh Burns
speeches.brief: The speaker expressed grave concerns about the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020, and argued that the Clean Energy Finance Corporation bill was pulled from debate because the National Party's amendment forced the government to instead reschedule the fair work bill.

speeches.speaker: Steve Georganas
speeches.brief: The Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 will weaken workers' rights, reduce job security, cut wages, and make wage theft harder to prosecute, representing a fundamental attack similar to John Howard's Work Choices.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Claydon
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fair Work Amendment (Supporting Australia's Jobs and Economic Recovery) Bill 2020 would cut pay for award workers by up to $11,000 per year, undermine the better off overall test, and nullify a Federal Court ruling on permanent casuals. Labor called for the bill to be rejected entirely, noting the government had already been forced to drop the test suspension due to crossbench opposition.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Fair Work Amendment Bill 2020, arguing it cuts wages, conditions and job security, and criticised the Morrison government and National Party for harming workers, especially in regional areas like the New South Wales North Coast.

speeches.speaker: Susan Templeman
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Fair Work Amendment Bill, arguing it would reduce job security, enable pay cuts, and weaken worker protections, similar to the Work Choices era. She criticised the JobMaker program for incentivising part-time over full-time work and noted the government only removed the BOOT test change due to lack of parliamentary support, not because it was unfair.
